findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Annual Treasury Management Review -( Full Council) 16th July 2026
findings.headline: Council executed £100m PWLB medium-term borrowing to finance capital expenditure and replace temporary funding
findings.detail: During 2025-26, the council raised £100m in new PWLB medium-term loans, financing capital expenditure and refinancing temporary borrowing. This brought total outstanding debt to £545.5m as at 31 March 2026, with annual interest payable of £20.3m.
findings.matters: A significant borrowing decision that shifts the council's debt from temporary to medium-term PWLB funding. This locks in debt service costs for an extended period and reflects the scale of capital spending the council is funding through long-term borrowing.
findings.figures: £100m PWLB loans, £545.5m total debt outstanding, £20.3m annual interest payable
findings.quote: The Council executed new PWLB medium-term loans of £100m to finance capital expenditure and to replace temporary borrowing.

findings.headline: Section 114 contingency is explicitly identified: if demand pressures prove ongoing or new pressures emerge, balanced-budget achievement may become impossible.
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states Section 114 is 'unlikely to be needed in the current year' but would be required if pressures are 'established to be on-going or there are new pressures'. This requires MTFS refresh. The council received up to £19m Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 based on conservative forecasts, but actual 2025/26 outturn was significantly better (£2.710m actual vs £15.315m forecast reserve use), suggesting EFS assumptions may require reset.
findings.matters: Section 114 notices are formal statutory warnings that a council cannot set a balanced budget and trigger intervention. The CFO's explicit flagging signals low margin for financial error and indicates that adverse demand or grant scenarios could rapidly escalate to statutory intervention.
findings.figures: EFS granted: up to £19m; reserve use forecast at budget time: £15.315m; actual reserve use: £2.710m
findings.quote: Section 114 is unlikely to be needed in the current year. If the pressures are established to be on-going or there are new pressures, they will need to be picked up in the MTFS refresh and potentially could result in a revised budget gap that would need to be resolved using reserves, savings or revised EFS assumptions.

findings.headline: Council Tax and Business Rates collection fell below target, with Business Rates collection described as having 'struggled'.
findings.detail: Council Tax collection achieved 94.79%, missing the 95% target by £402k. Business Rates collection achieved 94.6%, missing the 96% target by £1.033m. The Business Rates shortfall is attributed specifically to businesses struggling to pay following reduction of retail relief from 70% to 40%. Both underscore income volatility and resident/business financial stress.
findings.matters: Collection rates are self-controlled revenue sources. Declining collection signals either customer financial stress, which reduces future income, or collection effectiveness issues, both creating income volatility that must be hedged with reserves or savings.
findings.figures: Council Tax: 94.79% vs 95% target (£402k shortfall); Business Rates: 94.6% vs 96% target (£1.033m shortfall)
findings.quote: The in-year collection rate achieved in relation to Business Rates for 2025/26 is 94.6% (£69.803m), this is 1.4% (£1.033m) below the target of 96%. Collection has struggled this year with the drop in retail relief from 70% to 40% relief, with businesses struggling to meet the charges.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £14.320m will consume General Fund resources, with a further £10.340m deficit forecast for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £10.914m in-year, driven by growth in Education, Health and Care Plans and placement costs. Under statutory override the full £14.320m deficit carries forward. The DfE will fund 90% via Stability Grant, but the council must fund the remainder from General Fund. An estimated £10.340m further deficit is forecast for 2027/28, with no yet-announced treatment from DfE.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a permanent unfunded liability that drains General Fund resources each year to prop up schools' high needs provision. It reduces financial flexibility for other council services and reduces headroom for discretionary spending or borrowing.
findings.figures: In-year High Needs deficit: £10.914m; cumulative DSG deficit: £14.320m; forecasted 2027/28 High Needs deficit: £10.340m
findings.quote: The final position for the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) shows an in-year deficit of £10.914m in the high needs block. This would take the cumulative deficit for high needs to £19.786m at the end of March 2026, with an overall net DSG deficit of £14.320m.

findings.headline: Adults Social Care, Children's Services and Temporary Accommodation overspent by £23.8m, identified as ongoing structural demand pressures.
findings.detail: Adults and Transitions combined overspent by £10.905m; Temporary Accommodation overspent by £12.871m. These service areas are described as experiencing 'significant impact' from demand, 'in line with other Local Authorities' and 'London Boroughs'. The paper describes an overall unfunded directorate budget pressure of £25.231m — money the council spent but has not received funding for.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends are structural budget gaps, not one-off problems. They signal the council's baseline funding is insufficient for actual service obligations, meaning savings in other areas must continuously offset these pressures or the deficit grows.
findings.figures: Adults and Transitions overspend: £10.905m; Temporary Accommodation overspend: £12.871m; Total unfunded service pressure: £25.231m
findings.quote: The Council, in line with other Local Authorities, is experiencing high demand in relation to both Adults Social Care and Transitions and this has had a significant impact on the service outturn position with a combined overspend of £10.905m. In addition, in line with other London Boroughs there has been a significant overspend in relation to Temporary Accommodation (TA), with an overall overspend of £12.871m.

findings.headline: Budget Strategy Reserve depleted by 73% in a single year, from £13.965m to £3.704m.
findings.detail: Total drawdowns of £10.261m during 2025/26 included £2.216m for transformation programmes, £3.607m for earmarked reserves and provisions, £1.727m in other drawdowns, and £2.710m to fund year-end service overspends. The reserve now provides minimal buffer for unexpected pressures in 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: The Budget Strategy Reserve is the council's primary mechanism for managing in-year demand pressures and funding transformation. Its rapid depletion indicates the council has transitioned from managing financial risk to absorbing it reactively, leaving little capacity for further shocks.
findings.figures: Opening balance £13.965m; closing balance £3.704m; total drawdowns £10.261m
findings.quote: On the 1st of April 2025, the Budget Strategy Reserve (BSR) had a value of £13.965m. After drawdowns totalling £2.216m to fund the Transformation programme; a budgeted earmarked reserves and provisions drawdown of £3.607m; £1.727m in other drawdowns and a drawdown of £2.710m to fund the net service overspend, the balance in the BSR at 31st March 2026 is £3.704m.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability identified as material governance issue requiring ongoing action
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement explicitly identifies financial sustainability and audit assurance as material governance issues requiring ongoing action. The Council acknowledges its governance arrangements are under pressure from financial, operational and regulatory challenges. The specific nature of these sustainability concerns is not detailed in this summary.
findings.matters: A council flagging financial sustainability as a material weakness in governance signals potential budget control issues or underlying financial stress that affects creditworthiness
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: There are material governance issues requiring ongoing action, particularly: Financial sustainability and audit assurance

findings.headline: Pension scheme deficit of £208m requiring new triennial valuation at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The council's Local Government Pension Scheme has assets of £934m against liabilities of £1,142m, creating a material £208m deficit. A new triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 will be incorporated into the 2026 accounts. The auditors flag risk that small changes in actuarial assumptions (discount rate, inflation, mortality) could significantly affect pension liabilities and the potential asset ceiling.
findings.matters: A material pension deficit affects the council's balance sheet and financial sustainability. If assumptions change materially or the council enters pension surplus, it could shift reserves significantly. A lender needs to understand the pension obligation.
findings.figures: Assets £934m, liabilities £1,142m as at 31 March 2025. Deficit £208m
findings.quote: Fair value of defined benefit plan assets 934 [£m]... Defined benefit plan liabilities (1,142) [£m]

findings.headline: Significant prior audit evidence quality issues that will carry forward into 2025-26 audit
findings.detail: In the 2024-25 audit, the council experienced repeated delays in providing audit responses, provided transaction listings of inadequate quality (including contra-transactions that inflated work scope), and supplied audit evidence that was insufficient or inappropriate. The auditors could not conclude over some balances. These issues are documented as key areas for improvement requiring engagement with management.
findings.matters: Poor audit evidence quality signals weak financial controls and record-keeping. A lender needs assurance that the council maintains reliable financial records and responsive financial management. This also increases audit risk and cost.
findings.figures: Issues unresolved as of July 2026 audit plan publication
findings.quote: Some of the audit evidence provided by management was not sufficient and/or appropriate for the purposes of our testing. Some examples of this was evidence that lacked the clarity needed for the audit team to accept or an internally produced document would be provided which was not sufficient, appropriate audit evidence. Most often, this would result in the audit team rejecting the evidence and would require more time invested by officers and the audit team in gathering and reviewing evidence, reducing efficiency. However, this has also resulted in us being unable to conclude over the various balances.

findings.headline: Council has applied for Exceptional Finance Support from MHCLG to set a balanced 2026-27 budget
findings.detail: The council needed central government bailout funding to balance its budget for the coming year. This follows stated budgetary pressures in previous years. Without this exceptional grant, the council could not set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A lender considers exceptional support as a red flag. It signals that a council cannot live within its standard funding envelope and needs government intervention. This limits borrowing capacity and raises solvency questions.
findings.figures: EFS applied for to set balanced budget for 2026-27
findings.quote: The Council has faced budgetary pressures in previous years and has applied for Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) from the Ministry of Housing, Communities, & Local Government (MHCLG) to set a balanced budget for 26/27.

findings.headline: Council forecasting £32.97m services overspend mitigated by £17.66m underspends, leaving a net pressure of £15.32m in 2025-26
findings.detail: As at month 9 of 2025-26, the council's operational services are forecasting a significant overspend. While this is partially offset by corporate underspends and additional income, the net budget pressure of £15.32m represents material variance from the approved budget. The auditors' assessment is that the council is forecasting an immaterial deficit position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council can control spending within budget. A £15.32m net overspend (or £32.97m before mitigation) in a single year signals either spending control issues or that the budget was set incorrectly. This is live variance, not forecast.
findings.figures: Services overspend £32.97m, mitigated by £17.66m underspends, net pressure £15.32m
findings.quote: the Council has faced difficulties in delivering the 25/26 budget, with a forecasted services overspend of £32.97m as at month 9. This is mitigated by underspends and/or additional income of £17.66m in corporate budgets and therefore the net pressure is £15.32m.

findings.headline: Four consecutive years of unaudited accounts ended but assurance is still being rebuilt
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed opinions for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25. The auditors are now undertaking a separate rebuilding assurance process to re-establish confidence in previously unaudited periods. The auditors are still completing their rebuilding assurance risk assessment and will report separately once finished.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's accounts were verifiable. Four years of disclaimed opinions means nobody could verify the financial position. Even if the 2025-26 audit opinion is issued, the prior period history is material credit risk.
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25
findings.quote: For London Borough of Waltham Forest, this had the impact of two disclaimers of opinion, issued by your predecessor auditor, for the two financial years up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to your previously. For the 2024/25 external audit, we issued a disclaimer of opinion on 25 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council will receive £22m capital receipt in January 2027 to fund transformation costs and staff severance
findings.detail: The council is using Flexible Use of Capital Receipts to fund the 'cost of change' - transformation investment, redundancy and pension strain costs. This capital receipt is central to enabling the £40m+ savings through investment in change management and workforce restructuring. Close monitoring of return on investment is required.
findings.matters: This affects the council's cash flow timing and capital position. The January 2027 receipt date is material for understanding when funds become available for transformation spending. The model depends on delivering promised savings to justify the transformation investment.
findings.figures: £22 million capital receipt, January 2027
findings.quote: The Council will receive a capital receipt of £22 million in January 2027 and this will be utilised to fund both transformation costs and severance costs (i.e. both redundancy and pension strain) over the next two years.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support is explicitly time-limited, with financial sustainability target of 2029/30
findings.detail: The council has until 2029/30 (three years from this report) to achieve a balanced budget position without further government support. The paper describes this as 'a critical but time limited opportunity'. After that date, the council must be financially independent.
findings.matters: Time-limited support creates urgency and defines the deadline for transformation success. If the council fails to achieve sustainability by 2029/30, there is no indication of further government support available, creating risk for any lending decisions.
findings.figures: Deadline: 2029/30
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support offers a critical but time limited opportunity to stabilise the Council's financial position so that a balanced budget position can be achieved without the need for further support in the future.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: CIPFA Resilience Review found the council's previous 'salami-slicing' approach was insufficient and genuine transformation is needed
findings.detail: The November 2025 CIPFA review, commissioned as part of EFS preparation, identified that the council had relied on tactical and incremental cuts rather than systemic redesign. This suggests past financial management approaches did not work, explaining why EFS became necessary.
findings.matters: If a council has already tried cost-cutting without achieving sustainability, this indicates either past mismanagement or structural problems. The finding that deeper transformation is needed suggests the previous approach was inadequate and the challenges are more fundamental.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The review highlighted the need to move away from approaches that rely on 'salami-slicing' and tactical headcount reduction, rather than genuine, cross-cutting redesign.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council has already delivered over £140m in savings over the past decade
findings.detail: This history of substantial cost reductions means the council has exhausted many of the easier savings options. The paper notes that previous attempts used 'salami-slicing' and tactical cuts which proved insufficient, requiring deeper transformation now.
findings.matters: Previous savings of this scale indicate the council has limited fat remaining to trim. Future savings will be harder to find and more likely to impact service delivery or capacity.
findings.figures: over £140m savings delivered
findings.quote: After more than a decade of reduced funding from government and the delivery of over £140m savings, we need to radically rethink our offer if we are to achieve financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Seventy-two pence of every pound spent supports vulnerable services, with demand rising faster than resources
findings.detail: The council identifies this as one of three core realities driving financial pressure. Vulnerable services (social care, children's services, support for vulnerable adults) are demand-led and rising. This spending is largely uncontrollable by the council and creates structural budget pressure independent of council decisions.
findings.matters: Demand-led services are difficult to cut without policy change or service rationing. Rising demand on a fixed or declining budget means the structural deficit is likely to persist unless underlying demand patterns change or additional funding is provided.
findings.figures: 72p in every £1
findings.quote: 72p in every £1 the Council spends supports the most vulnerable, caused by demand continuing to rise faster than resources.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council must deliver £42.1m in savings over three years to achieve financial sustainability by 2029/30
findings.detail: The Mission Waltham Forest Transformation Programme targets £42.1m in savings over the next three years, with £40m+ coming from transformation activity. The council achieved £16.81m in the current year (2025/26) and is on track, but this sets the required pace for future years. The savings are based on a cost-of-change investment model.
findings.matters: This represents the scale of organisational change required. Lenders need to assess whether this savings plan is credible and achievable without undermining service delivery or financial position further.
findings.figures: £42.1m over three years; £40m from transformation; £16.81m achieved in 2025/26
findings.quote: Over the next three years, we will use this methodology to deliver £42.1m savings.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Waltham Forest has been granted Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG, placing it under government financial oversight
findings.detail: The council has received formal agreement for EFS from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. This is government support for councils in financial difficulty, indicating the council reached a point where it could not balance its budget without intervention. The support comes with specific requirements for transformation, governance, and delivery of savings.
findings.matters: EFS is a marker of serious financial stress and brings enhanced government scrutiny. Lenders need to understand that this council is under government intervention and has specific obligations to return to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: EFS level incorporated in 2026/27 Budget Report
findings.quote: MHCLG have agreed in principle the level of EFS as incorporated within the 2026/27 Budget Report.

findings.headline: Capital projects require additional Greater London Authority grant funding to address viability challenges and enable continued delivery
findings.detail: The council reports taking 'robust leadership' with construction and development partners to maintain project delivery despite challenging market conditions. This includes securing 'in principle agreement' to significant GLA grant funding and exploring alternative funding models specifically to address 'viability challenges'. This suggests projects are not financially viable at current costs without additional external funding.
findings.matters: Projects requiring external grant support to achieve viability indicates cost pressures on the delivery programme and dependence on ongoing government funding to meet capital objectives.
findings.figures: Significant level of GLA grant (unquantified in this paper)
findings.quote: This includes securing in principle agreement to a significant level of Greater London Authority (GLA) grant and exploring other funding models to address viability challenges and support continued delivery of the programme.

findings.headline: Capital Prioritisation Framework introduced in 2024 in response to high inflation, rising construction costs, and increased capital borrowing costs placing pressure on the Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.detail: In February 2024, Cabinet endorsed a new framework that restricts capital spending to schemes in construction, contractually obliged schemes, statutory compliance, schemes protecting the MTFS, and externally-funded projects. This framework was implemented specifically because inflation, construction cost rises, and increased borrowing costs had created unsustainable pressure on the council's medium-term finances.
findings.matters: The need to implement a restrictive capital prioritisation framework demonstrates that the council has had to constrain discretionary capital spending due to cost pressures, indicating financial strain.
findings.figures: Framework implemented February 2024
findings.quote: In February 2024, Cabinet endorsed the implementation of a new Capital Prioritisation Framework to support prudent financial management. The Framework was implemented in response to the risks of high inflation and rising construction costs, alongside increased capital borrowing costs, which have placed additional pressure on the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: Capital programme will cost £64.6 million in General Fund revenue over ten years, with £58.85 million of interest costs on borrowing
findings.detail: The finance section details the revenue implications of the capital programme, which are built into the MTFS. Interest costs alone are projected at £58.85 million over the decade to 2035/36, with an additional £5.75 million for Minimum Revenue Provision. This represents an ongoing revenue commitment arising from the capital programme's borrowing needs.
findings.matters: The substantial interest burden shows how much of future revenue budgets will be consumed by debt servicing, constraining flexibility for service delivery and other priorities.
findings.figures: £64.6 million total GF revenue cost; £58.85 million interest payable; £5.75 million MRP
findings.quote: Over the term of the Capital Investment Strategy (from 2025/26 to 2035/36), the GF revenue cost of the Capital Programme is estimated at £64.6 million, made up of projected interest payable of £58.85 million and MRP of £5.75 million.

findings.headline: Council applying for Exceptional Financial Support totalling up to £63 million across three years to manage revenue budget pressures
findings.detail: The council has applied for EFS of £19 million for 2026/27, an estimated £19 million for 2027/28, and £25 million for 2028/29. This support does not form part of the capital programme but impacts the council's borrowing needs and debt repayment obligations. The amounts indicate underlying revenue pressures beyond the council's normal budget capacity.
findings.matters: EFS applications signal that the council cannot balance its revenue budget within normal resources and requires government support, which indicates financial stress relevant to any lender assessing creditworthiness.
findings.quote: The council has made an application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £19 million for 2026/27, an estimated £19 million for 2027/28 and £25 million for 2028/29 to manage the estimated pressures on revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Supplier failures have begun occurring in the past year due to financial challenges and employer cost pressures
findings.detail: Several council suppliers have ceased trading during the past year, forcing the council to find mitigation and in some cases incur additional delivery costs at short notice. This is flagged as a new risk.
findings.matters: Supplier failure is a leading indicator of financial distress in the supply base. It signals that cost pressures are acute enough to be forcing exits, and suggests more may follow.
findings.figures: "A few" suppliers; no specific number given
findings.quote: During the past year, a few of the Council's suppliers have ceased trading due to their own financial challenges which also include the additional Employer costs.

findings.headline: North London Waste Authority plant replacement will create a cost cliff-edge within the next few years
findings.detail: The NLWA is replacing the facility that services the council. This will add significant financial pressure, potentially requiring service reductions to balance the budget. The council is using an NLWA smoothing reserve and has implemented food waste separation and recycling initiatives to manage levy share.
findings.matters: This is a committed future cost (plant replacement is happening) with no discretion. The timing and quantum are uncertain but material enough to flag as a strategic risk. The council has already achieved the lowest NLWA levy share in the authority area.
findings.figures: No quantum given; timing described as 'next few years'
findings.quote: The plant that services North London is being replaced which would add a significant financial pressure on the Council in the next few years. A cliff-edge in increased costs following the replacement plant would place significant pressure on the Council's budget and result in service reductions being needed to balance the budget

findings.headline: Delivery risk on agreed savings programme, with non-delivery potentially requiring use of reserves or further Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council acknowledges risk that agreed MTFS savings may not be achieved or slip into future years, and that the transformation programme may not deliver required savings. The 2026/27 budget includes a £12m contingency, partly to cover savings slippage.
findings.matters: If savings don't land, the budget immediately moves from balanced to in deficit, consuming reserves. Given the £19m EFS dependency, this is a second point of failure with no mitigation beyond the £12m contingency.
findings.figures: £12m contingency includes buffer for non-delivery of savings
findings.quote: Agreed MTFS Savings are not fully achieved or slip into future years. The Transformation programme does not deliver the required savings to meet the MTFS funding gaps. Potential for additional in-year overspends and funding gaps requiring use of reserves to balance the budget.

findings.headline: Temporary homelessness accommodation costs exceed government funding by design, requiring general fund subsidy
findings.detail: Local Housing Allowance is frozen and does not cover the full cost of temporary accommodation. The council has absorbed this funding gap from general reserves for both 2024/25 and 2025/26. The council reports no families currently housed in commercial hotels after securing additional properties.
findings.matters: This is a statutory duty that the council cannot refuse, and the funding gap is structural (government-frozen allowance vs rising market rents). It directly erodes reserves unless the council can reduce the number of households requiring temporary accommodation.
findings.figures: LHA frozen; impact material enough to flag in budget pressures 2024/25 and 2025/26
findings.quote: Increased demand & cost of accommodation has had a significant impact on the service budget pressure for both 2024/25 and 2025/26. The Local Housing Allowance (LHA) has been frozen again and this does not cover the full cost so the balance has to be funded from the general fund.

findings.headline: Adult social care costs rising 7% in recent months with no funding match, compounded by high-needs SEND demand growth
findings.detail: Care placement costs increased 7% between 2024/25 outturn and December 2025. The High Needs budget is "continuing to be challenging in-year" with SEND services showing growth in both demand and complexity. The council has begun external consultancy procurement to manage demand.
findings.matters: Social care is the largest spend for most councils and demand-driven cost pressures are hard to manage. A 7% increase in unit costs signals cost of care is outpacing inflation allowances in the budget.
findings.figures: 7% increase in weekly average care costs December 2025 vs 2024/25 outturn
findings.quote: The weekly average cost of care across all placement types is a 7% increase in December 2025 compared to the 2024/25 outturn position. The High Needs budget continues to be challenging in-year and SEND services continue to see a growth in demand, impacting both the general funds and High Needs Block.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget is contingent on £19m Exceptional Financial Support from central government, with Section 114 as fallback if refused
findings.detail: The council's balanced budget for 2026/27 depends entirely on securing £19m Exceptional Financial Support. If central government does not agree, the Chief Finance Officer would likely be required to issue a Section 114 notice, which would then require service cuts or additional funding.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal insolvency declaration that severely constrains a council's financial independence. This is the single point of failure in the council's budget planning.
findings.figures: £19m Exceptional Financial Support application
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the proposed budget presents a balanced budget position following an application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £19m from central government and is contingent on that being agreed. If the EFS of £19m was not agreed by central government, it would put the MTFS under significant pressure, in particular the level of reserves and the Chief Finance Officer might be required to issue a S114.

findings.headline: Budget Strategy Reserve of £14m fully utilised in 2025/26 to cover service overspend
findings.detail: The council forecasts that a £14 million Budget Strategy Reserve will be 'fully utilised in 2025/26 to mitigate the service overspend position and fund the resources required for the transformation programme.' This dedicated reserve created specifically to manage budget strategy risk is being consumed in the current financial year to cover overspends.
findings.matters: Deploying a dedicated risk reserve to cover current-year overspends demonstrates the council is managing pressures reactively rather than through budget control, and removes a tool available for future year management.
findings.figures: £14 million Budget Strategy Reserve
findings.quote: A budget strategy balance of £14 million is forecast to be fully utilised in 2025/26 to mitigate the service overspend position and fund the resources required for the transformation programme

findings.headline: Multiple high-risk pressures identified for MTFS period including schools in financial difficulty and High Needs Block deficit
findings.detail: Section 4.3 lists increasing financial risks during the MTFS period, including 'The number of schools in financial difficulty due to budget pressures arising from inflationary pressures and / or loss of income from falling rolls' and 'The level of deficit to the High Needs Block and potential lack of mitigations by the service' with a backstop date currently set at 31 March 2028. Additional risks include growth in demand for social care, temporary accommodation, and SEND.
findings.matters: Schools deficits and High Needs Block deficits flow to the general fund if schools close or the backstop mechanism triggers, creating unbudgeted liabilities. Combined with demand growth in social care and temporary accommodation, these pressures could exceed the council's ability to manage them from reserves or savings.
findings.figures: High Needs Block backstop date: 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The number of schools in financial difficulty due to budget pressures arising from inflationary pressures and / or loss of income from falling rolls within the primary sector. The costs of redundancy for both support staff and teachers will have to be funded from the general fund plus any residual deficit, if a school were to close or academise

findings.headline: £22m of capital receipts being used to fund revenue transformation spending
findings.detail: The council is deploying flexible capital receipts to fund transformation programmes that are intended to deliver future savings. The document states 'It is anticipated that the flexible use of capital receipts of £22 million will fund investment resources that will deliver the required savings and the transformation programmes.' This is a one-off use of capital resources to fund revenue transformation.
findings.matters: Using £22m of capital receipts for revenue transformation spending commits non-renewable resources and depends on transformation programmes delivering promised savings. If savings do not materialise, the council will have depleted capital and still face deficits.
findings.figures: £22 million flexible capital receipts
findings.quote: It is anticipated that the flexible use of capital receipts of £22 million will fund investment resources that will deliver the required savings and the transformation programmes

findings.headline: Forecasted funding gap in 2027/28 and 2028/29 with ongoing structural deficits
findings.detail: The current MTFS forecasts a funding gap will persist in years two and three of the three-year settlement period (2027/28 and 2028/29). The document also states the council is 'anticipating that there will still be a need to fund underlying structural deficits' in this period, suggesting the shortfall is not temporary but reflects structural imbalance between income and spending.
findings.matters: A forecasted funding gap extending beyond the current year means the council's financial challenges are not one-off but structural. This raises questions about sustainability and whether planned savings will deliver.
findings.figures: Funding gap forecast for 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.quote: The current MTFS is forecasting a funding gap in 2027/28 and 2028/29 and is also anticipating that there will still be a need to fund underlying structural deficits

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) required to balance budget across MTFS period
findings.detail: The document states that 'The application for EFS will provide sufficient funding to manage the net funding pressures and retain an available level of reserves' for 2026/27 to 2028/29. This indicates the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources and revenue alone without exceptional government support. The document also notes that 'it is likely that EFS will also be required in the MTFS period but will be reviewed on an on-going basis.'
findings.matters: Requiring exceptional government funding to balance the budget signals structural financial difficulty. Reliance on EFS is temporary and does not resolve underlying pressures, creating ongoing refinancing risk.
findings.figures: EFS applied for 2026/27 to 2028/29 MTFS period
findings.quote: The application for EFS will provide sufficient funding to manage the net funding pressures and retain an available level of reserves (including the general fund working balance)

findings.headline: General Fund Reserves falling sharply: £57.7m to £23m over two years
findings.detail: General Fund Reserves are forecast to fall from £57.7m in March 2025 to £26.4m in March 2026 (a £31.3m decrease) and then to £23m in March 2027 (a further £3.3m decrease). The document states this is 'due to the need to fund the underlying service pressure reported as part of the monitor and the need to invest in service improvements and future savings.' The working balance remains at £14.9m, which the Chief Finance Officer considers reasonable but represents just 4% of net budget.
findings.matters: A 60% decline in reserves in two years signals financial stress. The council is drawing down accumulated reserves to manage current-year overspends, reducing its buffer for unexpected shocks.
findings.figures: £57.7m (March 2025) → £26.4m (March 2026) → £23m (March 2027); Working Balance £14.9m
findings.quote: a decrease of £31.3 million compared to the balance as at 31 March 2025 and a decrease of £3.3 million projected in 2026/27, leaving a balance of £23 million as at 31 March 2027

findings.headline: Council drawing down Budget Strategy Reserve in 2025/26 to balance the current budget, with planned replenishment only in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Budget Strategy Reserve is being drawn down in 2025/26 (£3.4m-£4.4m depending on version). A drawdown in the current year signals the budget is not balanced from operations alone. The planned 2026/27 reversal suggests the council expects a small surplus that year, but this will be consumed if the forecast demand pressures or grant cliffs worsen.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns erode financial resilience and signal structural budget stress; excessive use of reserves suggests the underlying budget is not sustainable
findings.figures: Drawdown from Budget Strategy reserve 2025/26: £3,354k; additional drawdown: £838k; replenishment in 2026/27: £4,395k
findings.quote: Drawdown from Budget Strategy reserve 2025/26 (3,354) (4,395) 4,395... Additional BSR drawdown 24/25 (add pressures) 838 838

findings.headline: Service demand pressures spike to £19.3m in 2026/27, likely from social care, narrowing budget flexibility
findings.detail: Growth in service demand jumps from £5.9m in 2025/26 to £19.3m in 2026/27—more than three times the prior year. Demand then moderates but remains significant. Coupled with the grant funding cliff, this demand spike will compress the budget in exactly the year where new grants end.
findings.matters: If demand growth materializes as forecast while grants are ending and savings tail off, the council will lack the tools to manage the 2027/28 and 2028/29 shortfalls
findings.figures: Growth in service demand: £5,855k / £5,855k / £19,326k / £3,692k / £2,144k
findings.quote: Growth in service demand 5,855 5,855 19,326 3,692 2,144

findings.headline: New savings programme delivering £9.1m in 2025/26 reduces to zero by 2028/29, narrowing options for future budget pressures
findings.detail: The 2025/26 savings programme of £9.1m drops to £3.4m in 2026/27, then £1.2m in 2027/28, and disappears entirely by 2028/29. This sharp decline suggests savings are one-off in nature or that the council expects to exhaust easily-achieved efficiencies. With unresolved shortfalls appearing in 2027/28, the inability to sustain savings is material.
findings.matters: If the council cannot deliver sustained savings, it will have no mechanism to close the budget gaps already forecast in years 3 and 4 of the plan
findings.quote: Add in new 2025/26 savings programme (9,134) (9,134) (3,361) (1,203) 0

findings.headline: Social Care Grant (£27.5m) and other time-limited grants end after 2025/26, with no replacement funding identified
findings.detail: Multiple grants that funded the 2025/26 budget expire: Social Care Grant (£27.5m), ASC Market Sustainability & improvement Grant (£4.8m), CSC Prevention Grant (£1.3m), and Grant to cover NI costs (£2.2m) all drop to zero from 2026/27. The council's funding from government narrows materially. The Revenue Support Grant does increase significantly in 2026/27, but the gap from lost targeted grants is not fully offset.
findings.matters: A loss of time-limited grants of this scale (£35m+ annually) to a council with a £600m+ budget is a material funding cliff; the council's ability to sustain service levels depends on whether other funding or efficiency gains offset this
findings.figures: Social Care Grant: (27,548) to 0; ASC Market Sustainability: (4,763) to 0; CSC Prevention Grant: (1,345) to 0; NI grant: (2,183) to 0
findings.quote: Social Care Grant (27,548) (27,548) 0 0... ASC Market Sustainability & improvement Grant (4,763) (4,763) 0 0... CSC Prevention Grant (1,345) (1,345) 0 0... Grant to cover NI costs (2,183) (2,183) 0 0

findings.headline: The MTFP shows unresolved shortfalls of £19.3m in 2027/28 and £4.6m in 2028/29 with no identified funding solution
findings.detail: The budget reconciliation table shows the council balancing 2026/27 but then falling into unexplained shortfalls in years 3 and 4 of the plan. No mitigation is shown. This suggests either the savings programmes and service changes needed have not yet been finalized, or there is genuine uncertainty about how these years will be funded.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see how a council will close budget gaps; shortfalls in a published MTFP suggest unresolved financial stress in the medium term
findings.figures: £19,309k shortfall 2027/28; £4,620k shortfall 2028/29
findings.quote: (Shortfall)/Surplus 0 0 0 (19,309) (4,620)

findings.headline: Month 9 underlying service overspend forecast at £32.9m, with key pressures in Adults/Children Social Care and Temporary Accommodation unresolved despite mitigations
findings.detail: As of Month 9 (2025/26 financial year), the council is forecasting a £32.973m in-year service overspend. The largest pressures are in demand-led services: Adults and Children's Social Care, and Temporary Accommodation. While the council has implemented 'management actions' (expenditure panels, in-house foster carers, prevention services), these have not arrested the underlying trend. The overspend is being offset by corporate underspends and Business Rates Pool income—both of which are one-off or ending (the Pool is no longer viable after 2025/26). This suggests structural pressures are being masked by temporary mitigations.
findings.matters: A current-year overspend of this magnitude in Month 9 signals that the 2026/27 budget (even with EFS) may not hold. If the council cannot stay on track in 2025/26, confidence in 2026/27 projections is weakened.
findings.figures: Underlying service overspend Month 9: £32.973m; offsets from corporate underspends and Business Rates Pool income used to manage position
findings.quote: The Council is forecasting a £32.973 million in-year service overspend as at Month 9. The overspends are in key demand areas, including Adults and Children's Social Care and Temporary Accommodation.

findings.headline: Council tax now 45% of Core Spending Power (CSP), up from 35% in 2010/11; council tax base growing only 0.3% annually, far below inflation
findings.detail: The council is becoming increasingly dependent on council tax revenue. In 2010/11, council tax was 35% of CSP; by 2026/27 it is projected to be 45%, and 46-47% in following years. Meanwhile, the council tax base is growing at only 0.3% annually (0.5% in 2027/28 and 2028/29)—well below inflation. The government's CSP assumptions predict 1.9% annual base growth, but Waltham Forest's actual position is lower. The council is proposing 4.99% council tax increases to reach the threshold where referendum is required. This dependency is unsustainable if base growth continues to lag.
findings.matters: Councils with high council tax dependency and slow base growth are exposed. Unlike business rates or government grants, council tax is politically sensitive and residents can resist increases. If base growth stalls further, the council will be forced to cut services or increase borrowing.
findings.quote: Council tax as a % of CSP was 35% in 2010/11 and is anticipated to be 45% in 2026/27, 46% in 2027/28 and 47% in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Planned £42.1m savings over MTFS period face delivery risk; council applies 20% lag on savings delivery and 10% risk on service overspends in sensitivity testing
findings.detail: The council plans £42.113m savings: £18.594m in 2026/27, £15.761m in 2027/28, and £7.758m in 2028/29. However, to 'determine a prudent level of risk in delivering the budget, sensitivity analysis was applied to the savings delivery profile and service overspends. Therefore, a lag of 20% on delivery of savings and 10% risk on service overspends has been applied.' This means the council's own forecasting assumes only 80% of planned savings will actually materialize. Given that service pressures total £32.973m in-year overspend at Month 9, this is a significant credibility risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that stated savings will be delivered. The council's own sensitivity testing assumes 20% of savings will slip, which suggests either past non-delivery or uncertainty about future savings prospects. This reduces confidence in the MTFS.
findings.figures: Total planned savings £42.113m; 2026/27 £18.594m; 2027/28 £15.761m; 2028/29 £7.758m; sensitivity assumes 20% lag on delivery
findings.quote: To determine a prudent level of risk in delivering the budget, sensitivity analysis was applied to the savings delivery profile and service overspends. Therefore, a lag of 20% on delivery of savings and 10% risk on service overspends has been applied.

findings.headline: School reserves crisis: 21 of 44 maintained schools forecast in deficit by end 2025/26; opening balances declining 86% from £5.1m to £0.7m
findings.detail: Maintained schools brought forward opening balances of £5.1m in April 2025, projected to decline by 86% to £0.7m by end 2025/26. Schools in deficit increased from 19 in 2024/25 to 21 projected in 2025/26. This reflects falling pupil numbers (2.1% decline) combined with fixed costs and pay inflation. The Schools Block includes pay-related inflation but excludes general NFF increases, leaving schools to absorb pressures.
findings.matters: School deficits are a leading indicator of council-wide financial stress. Schools cannot borrow, cannot cut core services, and deficits quickly force intervention. This signals wider affordability problems affecting residents and potentially future council liability.
findings.figures: School reserves: £5.1m (Apr 2025) to £0.7m projected (end 2025/26); schools in deficit: 21 of 44; pupil numbers down 2.1%
findings.quote: The Council maintained schools had brought forward opening balances totalling £5.1 million in April 2025 and as per the latest projections, these balances are projected to decline by 86% to £0.7 million by the end of 2025/26. In 2024/25, 19 of 44 schools were in deficit and these are projected to increase to 21 in 2025/26.

findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG deficit forecast at £18.3m; cumulative DSG deficit £14.8m; statutory override protecting councils ends March 2028—after which council must fund deficit
findings.detail: The High Needs Block (funding for special educational needs and disabilities) has a projected deficit of £18.336m at 31 March 2026. The cumulative DSG deficit is £14.843m. EHCPs (Education, Health and Care plans) are growing: 3,812 children at 31 March 2025, rising to 4,022 by 31 December 2025 (6% in-year). Currently, a statutory override separates DSG deficits from the general fund. However, the override ends in March 2028, and government said it will 'centrally fund the full cost of SEND provision from 2028/29'—but this is not confirmed and there is 'a significant risk to the Council's MTFS if it is required to fund the current High Needs block deficit by 2028.'
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is hidden from the council's official financial position by the statutory override—but only until March 2028. At that point, a £18m+ liability could hit the general fund. The government has not confirmed it will absorb this cost, and the SEND white paper is still pending.
findings.figures: High Needs Block deficit £18.336m; cumulative DSG deficit £14.843m; EHCPs 4,022 at Dec 2025 (6% in-year increase); statutory override ends March 2028
findings.quote: the government will centrally fund the full cost of SEND provision from 2028/29. The government has not stated how existing liabilities will be dealt with at the end of the statutory override. However, the SEND white paper has not yet been released and may mitigate the risk if the Council were required to fund the current High Needs block deficit by 2028.

findings.headline: General fund reserves forecast to fall from £70.2m to £32.5m in one year; council acknowledges reserves are 'one-off in nature' and cannot be permanently replaced
findings.detail: Total reserves at 31 March 2025 were £70.222m; forecast for 31 March 2026 is £32.543m—a consumption of £37.7m in a single year. The council explicitly recognizes these are one-off buffers: 'the Council recognises that these reserves are only one-off in nature and must be replaced with permanent savings that will ensure the Council achieves financial sustainability.' With a required general fund working balance of £14.906m, usable reserves are tightening rapidly. The council holds £12m contingency for unforeseen events in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves at this rate indicates the council is funding operations with one-off cash rather than sustainable income. Once reserves are consumed, the only option is further service cuts or default. The council has limited headroom.
findings.figures: Reserves: £70.222m (31 Mar 2025) to £32.543m (forecast 31 Mar 2026); general working balance required £14.906m; contingency reserve £12m
findings.quote: the Council recognises that these reserves are only one-off in nature and must be replaced with permanent savings that will ensure the Council achieves financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care client numbers up 5.8% in-year to 3,744; 13% growth over three years; average weekly cost per client up 7%
findings.detail: ASC is 62% of the council's budget. At December 2025, 3,744 clients received funded support (5.8% increase from 3,537 in 2024/25). This continues a trend of 10% growth over two years and 13% over three years. The average weekly cost of care increased 7% at December 2025 compared to 2024/25 outturn. 'External placement and package costs for working age and older people continue to generate increased pressures.' The council is tightly managing through weekly expenditure panels but demand is relentless.
findings.matters: Demographic-driven demand for social care is rising faster than inflation or savings delivery. This is a permanent structural cost increase that will not reverse and represents an open-ended liability without national intervention.
findings.figures: 3,744 clients at December 2025 (5.8% increase); 10% increase past two years; 13% past three years; average weekly cost up 7%
findings.quote: the number of people needing support is rising, alongside the costs of providing this support. For Adult Social Care (ASC), the numbers of clients receiving funded support in 2025/26 is approximately 3,744 (as of December 2025) which represents an increase of 5.8% from last year (3,537 clients in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation cost per household surged 37% in two years; households in TA up 80% since April 2023, creating £14.5m budget pressure
findings.detail: Waltham Forest faces unprecedented homelessness pressure. The average weekly net cost of TA rose sharply from £199 in December 2023 to £272 in November 2025 (37% increase). Household numbers jumped from 858 in April 2023 to 1,581 by March 2025 (80% increase). Current forecast cost is £22.982m with a £14.452m budget pressure—this alone is one of the council's largest single pressures. The council has avoided commercial hotels for 10 months but notes 'reduced move-on options due to limited housing supply and wider affordability constraints.'
findings.matters: TA costs are demand-driven and hard to control; they now represent ~40% of the Housing General Fund budget. Runaway TA costs have triggered financial failures in other London councils and represent the largest uncontrollable pressure on this authority.
findings.figures: Average weekly cost £199 (Dec 2023) to £272 (Nov 2025); households 858 (Apr 2023) to 1,581 (Mar 2025); 2025/26 budget pressure £14.452m; forecast cost £22.982m
findings.quote: The average weekly net cost of TA to the Council has risen sharply, increasing by almost 37% from £199 in December 2023 to £272 in November 2025.

findings.headline: Structural deficit requires government bailout; £19m exceptional financial support needed to set balanced 2026/27 budget, with further £19.3m and £23.9m projected for following years
findings.detail: The council applied for £19 million Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2026/27, contingent on government approval (expected end February 2026). The Chief Finance Officer states this is 'not a sustainable financial strategy'. Without it, there would be a £19.044 million budget gap. Future years show increasing EFS need: £19.309m (2027/28) and £23.929m (2028/29). The council describes a 'structural deficit' and explicitly states it 'does not believe that it will be able to balance our budget over the long term without changing the way it operates.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can return to financial sustainability without permanent government support. These figures show the council cannot balance its budget through operational means alone and faces multi-year structural problems.
findings.quote: the Council does not believe that it will be able to balance our budget over the long term without changing the way it operates.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Treasury Management Strategy Report- Full Council 26th February 2026 v.2
findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position, funding capital through reserves rather than new borrowing
findings.detail: Waltham Forest is not fully borrowing against its Capital Financing Requirement, instead using cash from reserves and balances to fund capital programmes. The council describes this as a temporary measure and will adjust based on interest rate monitoring.
findings.matters: Understanding how the council finances capital investment reveals reserve position and borrowing headroom. An under-borrowed position indicates available reserves but may signal caution about future borrowing appetite or capacity.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement not fully funded with loan debt
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: CFO's statement on reserve adequacy is heavily conditional on EFS approval and delivery of unproven savings programmes
findings.detail: The CFO states the council 'has adequate reserves for the next 12 months' only subject to: EFS request of £19m being approved; services delivering management actions to reduce overspend; MTFS savings being identified and delivered; and no major unforeseen shocks. These conditions reflect uncertainty about both funding (subject to government approval) and execution (subject to service delivery).
findings.matters: Conditionality reveals the CFO cannot provide unconditional comfort on reserve adequacy; any delay in EFS approval, any shortfall in savings delivery, or any shock to demand instantly erodes the already-thin cushion.
findings.figures: £19m EFS required for 12-month adequacy, £32.973m 2025-26 overspend, £19.371m earmarked reserves
findings.quote: has adequate reserves for the next 12 months, subject to any major unforeseen unfunded burdens or shocks and only if the EFS request of £19m is approved by MHCLG.

findings.headline: CFO expresses uncertainty on organisational capacity to deliver transformation programme and manage identified savings, flagging risk to budget delivery
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly warns: 'there is a risk here, that there is insufficient organisational capacity and ability to transform quickly enough, which must be addressed for this budget to be delivered.' The 2026-27 budget relies on £31.848m of savings across 2026-27 to 2028-29 and multiple demand-reduction transformation programmes, but the council lacks demonstrated capacity to deliver at pace.
findings.matters: Acknowledged gaps in delivery capacity mean the council's financial plan depends on execution risk it has itself flagged as uncertain; non-delivery cascades directly to reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £31.848m savings identified for 2026-27 to 2028-29, multiple transformation programmes required to manage demand growth
findings.quote: However, there is a risk here, that there is insufficient organisational capacity and ability to transform quickly enough, which must be addressed for this budget to be delivered. Action must be taken by all senior officers, for the Council's finances to be sustainable over the MTFS period.

findings.headline: MTFS forecasts funding gaps of £19m in 2027-28 and £24m in 2028-29 with Fair Funding settlement providing only 4.2% and 4.1% increases against demand-led service growth of 5%+ annually
findings.detail: The council's MTFS shows a net funding gap of £19m in 2027-28 and £24m in 2028-29. The Fair Funding Review settlement provides only 4.2% funding increase for 2027-28 and 4.1% for 2028-29, whilst the council faces demand-led service increases: 5.5% EHCP increase, 5.8% Adult Social Care demand, and pressures across TA and Children's services all rising faster than funding.
findings.matters: Structural underfunding relative to demand indicates the council faces a sustained funding crisis that cannot be solved through one-off EFS requests or short-term management actions.
findings.figures: MTFS funding gap £19m 2027-28, £24m 2028-29, Fair Funding increase 4.2% (2027-28) and 4.1% (2028-29), demand growth 5.5%+ EHCP, 5.8% ASC
findings.quote: The Council's latest MTFS forecasts a net funding gap of £19m in 2027/28 and £24m in 2028/29, this gap can be reduced by further savings and efficiencies throughout the future MTFS periods and if not, then further applications for EFS will be required. The Fair Funding review has only identified a 4.2%% increase for the Council's funding in 2027/28 and 4.1% in 2028/29 which is insufficient to cover the inflationary and demand pressures across the majority of services.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care external placement costs rising sharply with at least three major service contractors entering administration in the past 12 months
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is receiving a £2.150m budget increase for 2026-27, including £1m for external placement cost shortfall and £0.9m for Disabled Facilities Grant, but the CFO notes the service must reduce costs which are high compared to peer councils. The CFO also reports that 'at least 3 major contractors to the Council in the last 12 months fall into administration', indicating market instability and supplier risk.
findings.matters: Contractor failures in social care disrupt service continuity, inflate emergency placement costs, and signal broader market fragility in a demand-led service the council cannot cut.
findings.figures: £2.150m budget increase to Adult Social Care, £1m external placement shortfall, £0.9m Disabled Facilities Grant shortfall, 3 major contractors in administration in last 12 months
findings.quote: Our social care (both Adults & Children's) supply base are already on the brink of bankruptcy, as we have seen at least 3 major contractors to the Council in the last 12 months fall into administration.

findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit of £9.464m in-year with cumulative DSG deficit of £14.843m poses risk of further reserve depletion if statutory override expires
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is running a £9.464m in-year deficit with cumulative net DSG deficit of £14.843m. The government has allowed 'negative' balances in reserves until March 2028, but if this statutory override is not extended, authorities must write off the negative balance immediately to the general fund. For Waltham Forest, this would not trigger section 114 immediately but would 'seriously deplete' reserves and increase likelihood of additional EFS or section 114.
findings.matters: A time-limited statutory exemption masks the true position; expiry of the override poses a cliff-edge reserve hit that is outside the council's control.
findings.figures: High Needs Block deficit £9.464m in-year, cumulative net DSG deficit £14.843m, EHCP numbers up 6%, statutory override expires March 2028
findings.quote: the high needs block deficit is forecast at £9.464m in-year and the cumulative net Dedicated Schools grant forecast deficit is £14.843m. If this was required to be written off, it would not immediately require a Section114 but would seriously deplete the Council's reserves and the likelihood of additional EFS request or Section 114 increases significantly.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand surged 80% in two years to 1,600 households with no additional budget provided and reliance on demand reduction not yet proven
findings.detail: TA numbers rose from 858 households in April 2023 to 1,581 by March 2025. The CFO describes this as 'the single biggest pressure facing the Council' but the 2026-27 budget provides no additional base funding, instead betting on demand reduction and management actions to contain costs. The council acknowledges that private rental market contraction and the Renters Rights Act pose risks to supply and cost projections.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled TA demand is the council's largest cost pressure with a track record of outpacing projections; failure to achieve planned demand reduction directly threatens the already-thin reserve position.
findings.figures: 1,581 households in March 2025 (from 858 in April 2023, 80% increase), current level 1,600 families, forecast £32.973m service pressure for 2025-26
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation continues to be the single biggest pressure facing the Council, with over 1,600 households at the end of December in need of emergency support. In April 2023, there were 858 households in TA, increasing to 1,581 by March 2025 - an increase of more than 80% in a two-year period.

findings.headline: Council reserves forecast to deplete by December 2026, requiring £19m in Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2026-27 budget
findings.detail: The CFO states the council must apply for EFS to balance the 2026-27 budget, and forecasts reserves will be depleted by December 2026. The council's total reserves have fallen from £126m in 2020-21 to £32.5m by March 2026, with earmarked reserves at just £19.4m (6% of general fund budget). The EFS request is described as in line with the council's previous estimate that it would require EFS within 18-24 months of February 2025.
findings.matters: A council requiring emergency government funding with imminent reserve exhaustion presents elevated refinancing risk and signals structural spending above income.
findings.figures: Reserves £32.543m (March 2026), earmarked reserves £19.371m, EFS request £19m, total reserves decline from £126m (2020-21)
findings.quote: we now forecast that our reserves will be depleted by Dec-26. Therefore, we will need to apply for Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) to balance the 2026/27 Budget, which is in line with the previous estimate by the Council that it would require EFS within 18-24 months of Feb-25 Budget setting report.

findings.headline: General Fund subsidizing temporary accommodation at £200-250 per week per household due to frozen LHA rates
findings.detail: Government subsidy for temporary accommodation is frozen at 90% of 2011 LHA levels (frozen again for 2026/27). Council funds the shortfall of £200-250 per week per household from General Fund. Private sector rents have risen 14-15% in London but LHA remains frozen, widening the gap.
findings.matters: Material and growing cost pressure on General Fund from housing pressures; indicates demand for temporary accommodation likely to remain high or grow; affects overall council financial position.
findings.figures: £200 per week minimum; 'more than £250 per week per household' subsidy cost; private rents up 14-15% in London
findings.quote: The council is only subsidised by government at 90% of the January 2011 LHA generating an average cost to the General Fund of over £200 per week per household in temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: Council is borrowing £166m over 10 years amid interest rate uncertainty and higher-for-longer rates
findings.detail: Capital programme includes £166m borrowing over the 10-year period (£41.1m in 2026/27). Council notes interest rates have remained higher than expected with risk of further delays to rate cuts, which will impact future borrowing costs and revenue budget.
findings.matters: Significant debt exposure with cost inflation risk; rising debt servicing costs will reduce financial flexibility and compete with service investment.
findings.figures: £166 million over 10 years; £41.103 million in 2026/27; higher interest and capital financing charges to follow
findings.quote: Interest rates have remained higher for longer than expected with an increasing risk that the Bank of England may delay further interest rate cuts, impacting the cost of borrowing.

findings.headline: Medium-term HRA funding gap: expenditure growing faster than income in 'extremely challenging' outlook
findings.detail: Council acknowledges the overall medium-term outlook for the HRA is 'extremely challenging', with expenditure on both revenue and capital forecast to rise faster than rental income available. The strategy focuses on efficiency improvements and reserve building to manage this gap.
findings.matters: Indicates structural financial pressure that may require service cuts, further rent increases beyond policy, or unsustainable reserve drawdowns over time.
findings.figures: Expenditure growth outpacing income growth; outlook described as 'extremely challenging'
findings.quote: The HRA's expenditure (on both revenue and capital) is forecast to rise faster than rental income available to it, creating a funding gap. Overall, the medium-term outlook for the HRA is extremely challenging

findings.headline: Rent convergence mechanism deferred to April 2027, losing £3m+ in expected 2026/27 income
findings.detail: Government announced rent convergence (additional rent increases above CPI+1%) would commence in 2026/27 but has deferred it to April 2027. The paper states this is 'disappointing' and that provisional estimates indicate over £3 million in additional income that was anticipated has been postponed.
findings.matters: Reduces financial flexibility for capital investment and service maintenance for the next year; demonstrates government policy uncertainty affecting long-term business planning.
findings.figures: more than £3 million in additional income deferred
findings.quote: While it is disappointing that convergence has been deferred until April 2027, provisional estimates indicate that the council could generate more than £3 million in additional income.

findings.headline: Mechanical & Electrical maintenance contract expires March 2027, requiring major re-procurement
findings.detail: A critical service contract (M&E) expires in March 2027 and requires a full re-procurement process. One-off costs and additional senior resource have been included in the budget to support the procurement. Key risks identified are market engagement and ensuring service continuity for tenants.
findings.matters: Service continuity risk; procurement in current market may face cost pressures; failure to secure replacement contract on time would affect essential housing maintenance.
findings.figures: Contract expires March 2027
findings.quote: The Mechanical and Electrical (M&E) contract expires in March 2027. To ensure continuity of service, the Housing Service will undertake a full re-procurement process.

findings.headline: Fire Safety Act, Building Safety Act, and Awaab's Law creating significant unforeseen cost pressures
findings.detail: Multiple recent regulatory requirements (Fire Safety Act 2021, Building Safety Act 2022, Social Housing Regulations Act 2023, and Awaab's Law from October 2025) have created unexpected capital and revenue cost pressures including increased planned and responsive repairs and admin costs.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs are eating into both capital and revenue budgets; indicates ongoing uncertainty around future compliance costs as regulations continue to tighten.
findings.figures: Significant unforeseen pressures (amounts not separately quantified)
findings.quote: additional regulatory and building and fire safety requirements have created significant unforeseen capital and revenue cost pressures, through increased planned and responsive repairs, and administrative costs.

findings.headline: High volume of disrepair legal claims placing strain on repairs budget
findings.detail: Council is managing a significant volume of disrepair claims with associated legal and remedial costs; budget for legal disrepair claims has been increased and additional resources brought in to improve performance. This is identified as an ongoing operational challenge.
findings.matters: Legal disrepair costs are consuming repairs budget and affecting service delivery; indicates potential housing stock condition or maintenance issues.
findings.figures: Budget increased; additional senior resource brought in
findings.quote: The council has had to manage a high volume of disrepair claims with associated legal and remedial costs placing further strain on the repairs budgets.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing assessed council at C2 grade in February 2025
findings.detail: An RSH inspection between December 2024 and February 2025 resulted in a C2 regulatory grade, which triggered the requirement to develop a robust Housing Asset Management Strategy. The council has now completed this strategy to rebalance investment priorities.
findings.matters: A C2 grade signals regulatory concern about the council's housing management and indicates the service requires closer oversight and improvement planning.
findings.figures: C2 grade
findings.quote: The council was inspected by the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) between in December 2024 and February 2025 and was assessed at a C2 grade.

news_drafts.headline: Council executed £100m PWLB medium-term borrowing to finance capital expenditure and replace temporary funding
news_drafts.lead: A significant borrowing decision that shifts the council's debt from temporary to medium-term PWLB funding. This locks in debt service costs for an extended period and reflects the scale of capital spending the council is funding through long-term borrowing.

news_drafts.headline: Section 114 contingency is explicitly identified: if demand pressures prove ongoing or new pressures emerge, balanced-budget achievement may become impossible.
news_drafts.lead: Section 114 notices are formal statutory warnings that a council cannot set a balanced budget and trigger intervention. The CFO's explicit flagging signals low margin for financial error and indicates that adverse demand or grant scenarios could rapidly…

news_drafts.headline: Council Tax and Business Rates collection fell below target, with Business Rates collection described as having 'struggled'.
news_drafts.lead: Collection rates are self-controlled revenue sources. Declining collection signals either customer financial stress, which reduces future income, or collection effectiveness issues, both creating income volatility that must be hedged with reserves or savings.
